steps.text: Write the "Technology and privacy" section of a Wikipedia article on airport privacy, covering the main screening and surveillance technologies used at airports and the privacy concerns each one raises.

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
### Body screening
- screening tech: harmful materials under clothes + consumed internally
- full body scanners / Advanced Imaging Technology (AIT), U.S. airports 2006
- two types used internationally: backscatters (high-speed, thin intensity x-ray beam, digital image) and millimeter wave scanners (3D image from reflected energy)
- June 2010 TSA commissioners report: framework for fundamental rights + health provisions
- extra privacy effects on disabled, transgender, older people, children, women, religious groups
- April 15, 2010 TSA letter: ~2000 body scanned photos from devices supposedly unable to store images
- alternatives: US and EU allow refusing screening -> pat-down; refuse pat-down -> no entry to secure area

### Baggage screening
- screening of all bags only after 9/11
- carry on: two stages, X-ray + manual inspection by Security Screening Operator (SSO)
- manual only if SSO has doubts
- after checkpoint: random searches; checked bags screened for explosives/dangerous items before flight

### Sniffer dogs/detection dogs
- used all over airports, esp. baggage claim
- role: stop drugs/explosives entering or leaving
- concerns over accuracy + physical capacity -> sniffer devices ("chemical sniffers", "electronic noses")
- odor unique to every individual; "body odor signature" -> gender, sexual orientation, health, diet; emotions (fear, happiness); biological footprint
- Lopez Ostra v Spain, European Court of Human Rights: odor affects privacy and human rights

### Camera surveillance and the future of facial recognition
- cameras placed strategically; more cameras -> more stored personal data
- human machine interface, operator assesses situation, decides where person appears on next camera
- facial recognition emerging, now part of camera surveillance
- Palm Beach airport study: low false alarm rate, almost 50% matching success
- Super Bowl use -> Fourth Amendment concerns

### Facial profiling
- 2003 TSA: Screening Passengers by Observation Technique (SPOT)
- behavioral recognition: facial expressions, body movement
- TSA Behavior Detection Officers (TBO) at checkpoints
- criticized: misidentified threats, intrusive searches on a hunch

### Biometric systems
- biometrics: unique, usually unchanging (fingerprints, speech, face)
- e-gates common, verify travelers via biometrics
- two privacy concerns: general vs system-specific (belief in system's ability to protect privacy)
- Europe first with e-gates; US heading toward e-gates
- US programs: Register Travel (RT), Global Entry (GE); expedite immigration for trusted travelers; fingerprint-based
- DHS: GE cuts wait time by 70%, almost no paperwork

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
### Body screening

Screening technology has gotten more advanced so that it can detect harmful materials under a traveler's clothes, and it can also detect harmful materials that a person may have consumed internally. Full body scanners, which are also called Advanced Imaging Technology (AIT), were introduced in U.S. airports in 2006. There are two types of body screening that are being used at all airports internationally right now, and these are backscatters and millimeter wave scanners. Backscatters use an x-ray beam that is high-speed but thin in intensity to make a digital image of a person's body. Millimeter wave scanners use millimeter waves and they make a 3D image from the energy that is reflected from the person's body.

In June 2010 a TSA commissioners report said that screening has to follow a framework so that fundamental rights and health provisions for travelers are ensured. Some groups have had extra negative effects on their privacy, including disabled people, transgender people, older people, children, women and religious groups. A letter from the TSA on April 15, 2010 stated that the TSA had about 2000 body scanned photos in its possession, from devices that they had claimed could not store data or images.

Travelers who want to opt out of body screening are offered alternative security measures. In the United States and the European Union a traveler can refuse the screening procedures and get a pat-down instead. But if the traveler also refuses the pat-down, then they are refused entry to the secure area of the airport terminal.

### Baggage screening

All bags entering the airport were not screened until after the 9/11 terrorist attacks. Carry on bags usually go through two stages of inspection, the first is an X-ray screening of what is in the bag and the second is a manual inspection by a Security Screening Operator (SSO). The manual inspection only has to happen if the SSO has doubts about what is in the bag. After the security checkpoints carry on bags can be inspected more through random searches, and checked in bags are screened for explosives or other dangerous items before they are sent to the passenger's flight.

### Sniffer dogs/detection dogs

Detection dogs are used all over airports, especially in the baggage claim sections. A detection dog's role is to stop substances like illegal drugs or explosives from going further into the facility or from leaving it. There have been concerns about the accuracy and the physical capacity of these dogs, and this has led to sniffer devices being created. These devices, also known as "chemical sniffers" or "electronic noses", are used like the dogs to detect any trace of drugs and explosives. Odor is not commonly thought of as connected to a person's privacy, but odor is unique to every individual. Every person has a characteristic odor called the "body odor signature" which can be used to identify gender, sexual orientation, health, diet and so on. It can show emotions like fear and happiness, and it is viewed as a biological footprint.

In Lopez Ostra v Spain the European Court of Human Rights ruled that odor does have an effect on privacy and human rights.

### Camera surveillance and the future of facial recognition
- cameras placed strategically; more cameras -> more stored personal data
- human machine interface, operator assesses situation, decides where person appears on next camera
- facial recognition emerging, now part of camera surveillance
- Palm Beach airport study: low false alarm rate, almost 50% matching success
- Super Bowl use -> Fourth Amendment concerns

### Facial profiling
- 2003 TSA: Screening Passengers by Observation Technique (SPOT)
- behavioral recognition: facial expressions, body movement
- TSA Behavior Detection Officers (TBO) at checkpoints
- criticized: misidentified threats, intrusive searches on a hunch

### Biometric systems
- biometrics: unique, usually unchanging (fingerprints, speech, face)
- e-gates common, verify travelers via biometrics
- two privacy concerns: general vs system-specific (belief in system's ability to protect privacy)
- Europe first with e-gates; US heading toward e-gates
- US programs: Register Travel (RT), Global Entry (GE); expedite immigration for trusted travelers; fingerprint-based
- DHS: GE cuts wait time by 70%, almost no paperwork

steps.text:
### Body screening

Screening technology has gotten more advanced so that it can detect harmful materials under a traveler's clothes, and it can also detect harmful materials that a person may have consumed internally. Full body scanners, which are also called Advanced Imaging Technology (AIT), were introduced in U.S. airports in 2006. There are two types of body screening that are being used at all airports internationally right now, and these are backscatters and millimeter wave scanners. Backscatters use an x-ray beam that is high-speed but thin in intensity to make a digital image of a person's body. Millimeter wave scanners use millimeter waves and they make a 3D image from the energy that is reflected from the person's body.

In June 2010 a TSA commissioners report said that screening has to follow a framework so that fundamental rights and health provisions for travelers are ensured. Some groups have had extra negative effects on their privacy, including disabled people, transgender people, older people, children, women and religious groups. A letter from the TSA on April 15, 2010 stated that the TSA had about 2000 body scanned photos in its possession, from devices that they had claimed could not store data or images.

Travelers who want to opt out of body screening are offered alternative security measures. In the United States and the European Union a traveler can refuse the screening procedures and get a pat-down instead. But if the traveler also refuses the pat-down, then they are refused entry to the secure area of the airport terminal.

### Baggage screening

All bags entering the airport were not screened until after the 9/11 terrorist attacks. Carry on bags usually go through two stages of inspection, the first is an X-ray screening of what is in the bag and the second is a manual inspection by a Security Screening Operator (SSO). The manual inspection only has to happen if the SSO has doubts about what is in the bag. After the security checkpoints carry on bags can be inspected more through random searches, and checked in bags are screened for explosives or other dangerous items before they are sent to the passenger's flight.

### Sniffer dogs/detection dogs

Detection dogs are used all over airports, especially in the baggage claim sections. A detection dog's role is to stop substances like illegal drugs or explosives from going further into the facility or from leaving it. There have been concerns about the accuracy and the physical capacity of these dogs, and this has led to sniffer devices being created. These devices, also known as "chemical sniffers" or "electronic noses", are used like the dogs to detect any trace of drugs and explosives. Odor is not commonly thought of as connected to a person's privacy, but odor is unique to every individual. Every person has a characteristic odor called the "body odor signature" which can be used to identify gender, sexual orientation, health, diet and so on. It can show emotions like fear and happiness, and it is viewed as a biological footprint.

In Lopez Ostra v Spain the European Court of Human Rights ruled that odor does have an effect on privacy and human rights.

### Camera surveillance and the future of facial recognition

Surveillance cameras are put around airports in strategic places to keep everyone safe. More camera surveillance means more personal data being stored. A person operates the surveillance system through a human machine interface to assess a situation. The operator is in control of the cameras and decides where the person will show up on the next camera. Facial recognition is an emerging technology for airport security, and facial recognition has now made its way into camera surveillance. A study at the Palm Beach airport found that face recognition surveillance had a fairly low false alarm rate and a success rate of almost 50% for matching. Using facial recognition at the Super Bowl raised concerns about the Fourth Amendment.

### Facial profiling

In 2003 the TSA introduced the Screening Passengers by Observation Technique (SPOT) to try to improve the detection of terrorist threats. SPOT is a behavioral recognition system that looks at how people act through their facial expressions and their body movement. TSA Behavior Detection Officers (TBO) are at airport security checkpoints and they watch for behavior from travelers that might suggest malice. SPOT has been criticized a lot for the times it misidentified a threat, which caused intrusive searches on travelers based only on a hunch by a TSA official.

### Biometric systems

Biometrics are human characteristics that are unique to each person and that usually do not change, like fingerprints, speech, face, etc. Electronic gates, or e-gates, are now very common in airports because they can verify travelers from their biometric information. There are two kinds of privacy concerns with e-gates, general privacy and system-specific privacy. System-specific privacy is about beliefs on whether the system is capable of protecting privacy. Europe was the first to introduce e-gates in its airports, and the future of airport technology in the United States is pointing toward e-gates.

The United States has two registered travel programs, the Register Travel (RT) system and the Global Entry (GE) System. These programs are meant to speed up immigration procedures for trusted travelers and they are mainly based on fingerprint recognition. Besides the security benefits, the Department of Homeland Security says GE Systems have reduced wait time by 70% and need almost no paperwork.
